ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 曰：不聞。成曰：汝既不聞，則此一喝是無，能入始教。又顧善曰：我初一喝，汝即道有。喝久聲消，汝復道無。道無則元初實有，道有則於今實無。不有不無，能入終教。又曰：我有一喝之時，有非是有，因無故有。我無一喝之時，無非是無，因有故無。即有即無，能入頓教。又曰：我此一喝，不作一喝用。有無不及，情解俱忘。道有之時，纖塵不立。道無之時，橫徧虗空。即此一喝，入百千萬億喝。百千萬億喝，入此一喝，是能入圓教。善不覺起立，向前作禮。成又曰：非惟一喝為然，乃至語默動靜，一切時、一切處、一切物、一切事，契理契機，周徧無餘。於是四眾歡喜，龍顏大悅。淨因可謂識佛意，通佛語，千差萬別，七縱八橫，辯才無礙。把這一喝，恁麼說出來，理上也著，事上也著，禪上也著，教上也著，喚作閙市裡颺碌磚，無有不著者。今日一會，却非偶然。建會華月窻與學般若菩薩，既在禪門，又通教相。欲報佛恩德，無過流通正法。而況獨芳和尚，久專講席，特重禪宗。山僧此來，不勝慶幸。因華嚴大教，發明臨濟禪。諸供養中，法供養最。喝一喝云：且道山僧適來一喝，與淨因一喝，相去多少？復喝一喝。珠維那請普說，師云：妙喜老人道：命根斷，家活大，法性寬，波瀾濶，乃是禪病科，立效散。你諸人要識命根麼？只是第八識。如今禪和子病痛、昏沈、掉舉，總在第八識中，若要獨脫無依，須是把第八識一刀兩叚，方始快活，教中所謂𢬵命不死難。僧問投子：大死底人却活時如何？投子云：不許夜行，投明須到。這僧問得能切，投子答得又親，伯牙與子期，不是閒相識。第八識既斷，蛇無頭尾不行，正賊斬了，論什麼賊黨？無始至今，來為先鋒，去為殿後，風動塵起，縈絆殺人，但得一念不生，自然前後際斷。便見溈山道：靈光洞耀，逈脫根塵，體露真常，不拘文字，心性無染，本自圓成，但離妄緣，即如如佛。僧也如如佛，俗也如如佛，來也如如佛，去也如如佛，盡十方世界無一人不是如如佛者，嫌箇什麼？欠少箇什麼？英靈衲子便好向這裏全身擔荷，不用回頭轉腦，特地起疑，疑佛疑祖，疑死疑生，如染一綟絲，一染一切染，如斬一綟絲，一斬一切斬。先聖苦口相勸，葢為袈裟同肩。己事明白，他事亦明白。己事了辦，他事亦了辦。豈可如獐獨跳，不顧後羣。既住佛屋，踏佛地，喫佛飯，著佛衣，須行佛行始得。且如何是佛行？佛讚者是佛行，佛訶者是魔法。說什麼尼薩耆波逸提，纔

Occurrences.Kwic: 中而用已成其體，如「玄德升聞，重華協帝」，此所謂「靈機弘聖道，真智利群迷」也，率賓歸王故。又謂之「共功同歸至化，即共樂無為之治」，亦謂「子全身紹父」，亦謂：「賓能為主」。兼中到者，即君臣道合也。以黑白渾融而體用一無分別，如堯舜之揖讓德成，舜先賓能相續為主，而堯退位又作主中主；堯既不居正位，舜亦不居偏功，此所謂「渾然無內外，和融上下平」也。亦謂之「功功」，是無功無不功也。亦謂之「父子恩忘，斧斫不開」，向上尊貴之正命，食亦不取矣！此秘密藏千聖不傳，豈言所可盡哉？示諸學人及眾居士示諸學人及眾居士予昔年常會吾漳戴，今梁觀察及予父弟于維揚舟中。戴公曰：「聞佛教有超凡入聖之說，師果能親證其旨乎？」予曰：「須深悟得游戲三昧可也。」公曰：「如何則能悟？」予曰：「公見夫戲子乎？在臺下即凡，在臺上即聖。」公曰：「何也？」予曰：「戲子在臺下，人或稱之：『你為人真周公、孔子。』戲子必大喜；人或毀之：『你為人真仲子、齊人。』戲子必大怒。及至登臺，則親身為周公、孔子卻不自喜；儼然仲子、齊人卻不自怒。吁！豈你真能為周、孔，而仲、齊亦豈你真不足為哉？此何以故？蓋彼臺下以無為有，故喜怒生；臺上以有為無，故是非泯。以無為有，故妄執成凡；以有為無，故妄解成聖。然則凡夫墮落與聖人超脫，只在一念有無之轉機也，而聖凡何曾有實法？乃迷悟自成其墮超耳！」公大喜曰：「此天下奇論，讀盡千言萬語，不如臺下臺上一念有無之轉機，而成聖凡之一語，令人開悟無迷，真痛快斬截也。」予父存三居士曰：「審如此語，則觀音所以三十二應者，非獲此如幻解脫法門乎？」予曰：「正是此意，第當局難得不迷耳，所謂卻來觀世間，猶如夢中事。若主人公心眼不惺，則未免又為夢幻空花所惑亂也。」予弟季玉曰：「瑋前日見《林間錄》載王文正公當大拜時，宴會官僚作戲，公題詩曰：『諸優戲場中，一貴復一賤；心知本是同，以故無欣厭。』覺範大師曰：『謂此老通身是眼，一點也瞞他不得。』正符此意。」予笑曰：「吾弟從此為人處世，須是眼睛鼻孔端正始得。」戴公曰：「善善！決不可少師末後者一錐劄也。」嗚呼！此予戊午年寓金陵天界，因戴公挽予過廣陵一番游戲時，吾徒大方、大圓二子侍側猶能記之，計今二十餘年，戴公與吾父弟皆作古人，可勝歎哉！我今重新舉似你諸學人及眾居士，果能忘軀為法，依止叢林參承師友，切不可於名言相法中妄生分別執取，而起是非、憎愛、冤親、苦樂之心，以自惑亂其身心性命；亦復惑亂他人之解脫知見也。予嘗示諸職事曰：「汝等參學，略能參破生滅妄想之麤跡，則自不為世間名言相法所顛倒也。我試令你首座今日退席為本堂侍者；即令本堂侍者立居首座之位。侍者儼然以首座自任；首座安然以侍者執持，毫無上下彼我之分，庶于解行少有證據。若纔令悅眾退下作副悅眾；令副悅眾退下作散單，便如奪了封侯印，心憤憤口悱悱，寧可知識不親覲、生死不參究，者個體面決不成得，特於半夜捲單而行，豈真有為法求依止善知識之心者乎？嗚呼！此天下弄虛頭好名，學人通病，以類推之皆若是也，雖有醫王亦當拱手矣！凡住叢林之人，毋論事之巨細，皆痛治偷心求親證，雖群居雜處，能使上下相忘于道術；凡聖相忘于戲游，何復有生死是非之能惑亂？又何慮身心性命之不超脫？」伏惟，珍重！示熊仁者示熊仁者舉：「雪關大師拈丹霞訪龐居士公案云：『龐公若無後語，幾乎被靈照喪卻家風。秪如道：「赤土塗牛奶。」意作麼生？不令蜂蝶誤認隔墻花。』」師云：「雪關師兄蹉過也，龐公雖是沒牙大蟲，其爪甚利；靈照如鸞鳳沖霄，隱顯莫測。于丹霞處明露秋光，于龐公處暗藏春色，不然何處見靈照機捷哉？熊仁者既已貞節自持，復能參悟自性，若於此淆訛處透得過，始有出身活路也。」更示之偈曰：「靈照把金針，妙密
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB174.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie. Juelang Daosheng remembers a conversation with a lay patron, his father and his younger brother about delusion and freedom as turns within a single thought, rather than fixed substances belonging to ordinary people or sages. His father connects this with Guanyin’s thirty-two forms of compassionate response. The younger brother cites a poem said here to have been written by Wang Wenzheng while watching actors at an official banquet: on the stage one is noble and another lowly, yet knowing their underlying sameness leaves no delight or aversion. Juelang warns his brother that his eyes must remain clear when dealing with people, then raises the memory again for his present students and lay hearers, urging them not to bind themselves and others through discriminatory attachment to words and appearances. The exact pair is the older lay poet's quoted voice, not the brother's own composition. Huihong's parallel calls that poet Wang Wengong, so the personal identity is left unresolved rather than forcing the two titles into one known man.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. Guxue Zhenzhe rejects several proposed ways of reaching truth: eliminating sight and hearing, shutting the eyes in stillness, or abandoning every activity. Raising his whisk, he asks whether the audience sees; penetrating here, he says, reveals flowing rivers, standing mountains, flowers and birds as openly manifest. He quotes the actors' noble and lowly roles together with the following lines about sameness and freedom from delight and aversion. At that point, he says, one can freely appear as emperor, minister, monk, layperson, boy or girl, even in remote villages, to help others recognize their own ground. He contrasts this wide benefit with merely relieving one place's temporary want and ends with talking stone tortoises and a snowy waterfall scattering heavenly flowers. The quoted stage image serves this present teaching about responsive roles; it is not an instruction that the hearers should seek a prestigious role or reject a humble one. The older poet remains the quoted speaker; Guxue supplies the current application.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB300.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong. Chaozong Tongren discusses Fenyang's questions about whether the teacher and student are the same or different and about the mysteries contained in one sentence. He warns that present time and the empty age are medicines given for an occasion, not separate realities to rank and grasp. He then quotes the actors' noble and lowly roles and their underlying sameness, saying that students who despise the present and prize the empty age turn the medicine into a disease. Understanding the one sentence's three mysteries, he says, lets medicine and disease both be forgotten. He goes on to describe his own recognition that present time and the empty age do not lie outside the present thought. Here the old stage poem is used against a particular hierarchy in the student's understanding; it is not itself a new doctrine that all distinctions should be confused. Chaozong is the current critic, while the exact couplet remains the unresolved earlier lay poet's voice.

Senses.Explanation: Among the actors on the stage, one is noble and another lowly. Juelang Daosheng remembers a conversation with a lay patron, his father and his younger brother about delusion and freedom as turns within a single thought, rather than fixed substances belonging to ordinary people or sages. His father connects this with Guanyin’s thirty-two forms of compassionate response. The younger brother cites a poem said here to have been written by Wang Wenzheng while watching actors at an official banquet: on the stage one is noble and another lowly, yet knowing their underlying sameness leaves no delight or aversion. Juelang warns his brother that his eyes must remain clear when dealing with people, then raises the memory again for his present students and lay hearers, urging them not to bind themselves and others through discriminatory attachment to words and appearances. Huihong's parallel calls that poet Wang Wengong, so the personal identity is left unresolved rather than forcing the two titles into one known man. Senses.PreferredTarget: What can be returned is not you; what cannot be returned, who else could it be?
SearchAliases: what can be returned is not you; what cannot be returned, who else could it be?
Senses.Note: In the Shurangama Sutra, what can be returned to its conditions is distinguished from what cannot be returned, and the listener is asked who that could be. Buhui replies with a verse about a bird, moon, and autumn water. Hanyue compares the sutra’s directness to a fruit offered whole that readers still cannot swallow. Neishao answers with a stage curtain image; Hansong places the question beside another verse on seeing. These uses keep the final “who?” as a present challenge.

Senses.Explanation: Having no route by which devas can offer flowers marks conduct with no exposed place for heavenly praise to fasten onto; the paired outsiders likewise find no opening to spy. Yuanwu Keqin uses the pair for one whose discriminating machinery is extinguished and whose conduct has become ordinary. Dahui Zonggao contrasts meticulous rule-keeping that earns heavenly food with the ancestral gate, where devas have no route to bring flowers. Chushi Fanqi uses it for unhindered conduct that neither clings to brightness nor liberation. Chaozong uses the image in his own opening-furnace sermon to describe unobstructed ordinary conduct. Mixing applies the image to his late teacher in his own memorial hall discourse.

Senses.Note: Bird Nest Daolin gives the pair to Bai Juyi as the heart of the teaching; the familiar response says that even a child can say it, while an old person may struggle to live it. Yongjue comments on that exchange. Tian'an writes the pair into a new verse, and Shanhui, Baichi, Jieweizhou, and Jiguang voice it in direct present answers. Jiguang uses it specifically to answer what ethical discipline is. These uses keep conduct, rather than verbal novelty, at the center.

Senses.Explanation: Two short commands direct the listener away from wrongdoing and toward good deeds. The Bird Nest and Bai Juyi exchange contrasts the saying's simplicity with the difficulty of living it. Later masters give the same pair as their own answer in sermons and direct exchanges.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Elsewhere they cremate; here I bury you alive.
AlternateTargets: Other places burn the dead; here I put you under alive.
Senses.Note: Linji says the pair after Huangbo has struck the monastery officer. Juelang uses it when a monk asks about living in the mountains, then strikes him. Miaoyun says it while heaping soil on a monk. Zhulang utters it while hoeing in answer to a road question. Eryin and Chulin separately judge Linji's exchange with Huangbo.

Senses.Explanation: The speaker opposes other places' cremation to burying someone alive here. In Linji's exchange with Huangbo, the violent image marks an immediate intervention rather than funeral instruction. Later masters make the pair answer actual visitors; one puts soil on a monk and another speaks from the hoeing ground.

Senses.Explanation: A collective address naming the corps of elder masters across the quarters — the standing whetstone every speaker grades his own gate against. Xuansha Shibei's address to the assembly presses the corps — the elders all say they meet beings and foster life, but meeting the blind, the deaf, and the mute, how will they meet them? fail there and the teaching has no proof — the case raised whole in Yunmen's record with the poke-and-call answer hard behind; Yangshan Huiji's proving device, told in Yuanwu's appraisal, lifts the whisk for every visiting monk — do the quarters still speak of this or not? set that aside: what do the elders mean? — the very claw and fang of the school in Guishan's praise; Fenyang Shanzhao closes an address on them — the elders, unable to do otherwise, talk east and west, the whole assembly crowding heads sleepless and calling it seeking: where will you go seek? work done outward is dullard's work; and Foyan Qingyuan, dying at fifty-four, tells his disciples the elders all leave a parting verse — can the world be bid farewell? where would one go? — and to the end, not one word. Xuedou Chongxian, weighing the Gushan sword case — the elders all say Gushan lost an eye, not knowing that under a heavy bounty there must be a brave man, though on close inspection all get buried at once — carried in Gulin Qingmao's re-raising, where the sword's own handle sits in the monk's hand; Chushi Fanqi wants none of their locked-room teaching — unlike the elders' hidden-room talk of the way, passed mouth to mouth and one man to one man, cold-spying the cauldron and furnace as they guard the school's lifeline — the true seeker must spit that food out; Jiqi Hongchu, at the work-day address, grants that the elders all say they meet beings and foster life — yet not knowing where the seven kitchen things come from, how would they know the carrying-baskets hidden in the miscellany store? — and hauls the lot out at once; and Yushan Shangsi rules the old man's roundabout a detour — the elders all meet beings and foster life, but you people are not blind, deaf, or mute: the whisk raised is plainly seen, the words plainly heard, the turning phrases plainly spoken — only do not stir this place.

Senses.PreferredTarget: If teachers elsewhere had the skill to hold one, there would be no arriving at Jingming today.
SearchAliases: if teachers elsewhere had the skill to hold one, there would be no arriving at jingming today.
Senses.Note: The arrival clause leaves its subject unstated. The article does not turn that compression into a fixed personal itinerary. The retained later readings disagree about the verse value, so neither is imposed as the only original intention.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua. In the small address at Jingming hermitage, Ying'an Tanhua gives a four-line verse invoking thirty-three prefectures and seventy monks, then roughly compares donkey cheeks and horse jaws. Its last pair says that if teachers elsewhere had a hand capable of catching and holding, there would be no coming to Jingming today. The image turns the presence at Jingming into a challenge to the adequacy of teaching elsewhere. The verse is pointed and compressed: it does not expressly state who is the subject of coming in the final clause, so the translation does not invent a complete personal journey for a particular monk. Ying'an is the original named speaker. Later witnesses show that even teachers who preserved the verse did not all agree about whether its pointedness was admirable.

Lüyan He raises Ying'an's four-line verse and says directly that such speech exalts oneself while belittling others. He offers his own version: the thirty-three prefectures and seventy monks are auspicious creatures vying with one another; all teachers elsewhere have catching hands, but getting clear of them belongs to a person beyond measure. Asked what that person is, he looks to either side and tells the assembly to drink tea after the gathering. The original headword is still Ying'an's quoted pair, not Lüyan's replacement, which changes its claim. This present reply therefore supplies a critical counter-reading to Yuejiang's praise: it shifts the test from declaring other teachers inadequate to the student's capacity to pass beyond their hold, ending with an ordinary instruction rather than another fixed definition.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J23/J23nB134.xml). Recorded Sayings of the Five Houses (Selections). The Lotus Scripture's Buddha speaks of all things' quiescent character as beyond verbal declaration, yet the Chan witnesses repeatedly put that claim beside actual speech and action. Yunmen Wenyan raises it as a teaching quotation and asks what speaking or not speaking there can be in the words being uttered now. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1440.xml). Chan Master Weilin Daopei’s Return to the Mountains Record. Senses.PreferredTarget: From their origin, all things bear the mark of stillness.
AlternateTargets: All phenomena have from the outset the character of quiescence.

Senses.Note: The inherited couplet comes from the Lotus Sutra. Fushi adds winter clothing to an older spring-flower response; Jiqi sets the line beside heaven, earth, and human activity; Wuchu adds the setting sun and rising sun; Hengchuan follows it with four seasons; Daian applies it to the conduct of a summer retreat. The exact verse belongs to Shakyamuni Buddha, while each current master supplies a separate application.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 拈拄杖，云：前四十五日已去，紅霞穿碧落；後四十五日未至，白日繞須彌。正當今日，上無衝天之計，下無入地之謀。卓一下，云：將軍射中南山虎，元是藍田老石頭。上堂，舉：僧問趙州：二龍爭珠，誰是得者？州云：老僧只管看。師云：者僧發此一問，大似向致仕宰相面前說少年登科事一般。只如道老僧只管看，又作麼生？雖無上馬力，猶有殺人心。上堂，拈拄杖云：行不到處行一步，甜瓜徹蔕甜；說不到處說一句，苦瓠連根苦。掃盡從前閑佛祖，發機須是千鈞弩。擲拄杖，下座。佛成道，上堂。拈拄杖，云：大眾！黃面老漢雪山六年受盡凍餓，將謂成得箇什麼？元來是眼裏著沙不得。便乃指空、話空、拏空、塞空。卓拄杖，云：千古萬古成狼藉，帶雨梅開濕曉風。應真宗師至，上堂：律非縛，禪非脫。蝴蝶夢莊周，周公制禮樂。會則事同一家，不會則萬別千差。還會麼？一片白雲生嶺上，幾回開了又還遮。上堂：春色融融，花氣濛濛。六牕俱不鑰，當處不留蹤。危欄同徧倚，身在寂寥中。幾欲全提先漏洩，滑唇黃鳥弄春風。上堂。諸法從本來，常自寂滅相，玉兔西沈，金烏東上。便與麼去，坐殺闍梨；不與麼去，走殺上座。拈拄杖畫一畫，云：石牛攔古路，一馬生三寅。佛涅槃，上堂。簸土揚塵，金剛正體。七顛八倒，大寂定門。擊拂子，云：排空煙嶂添愁色，著雨林花帶淚痕。法喜長老至，上堂：向上一路，啐󲣅猶乖。水乳和同，肝膽楚越。南嶽問馬師作麼生？巴陵呈雲門三轉語，意在於何？遺腹之子，無貌於心。上堂。見見之時，雨洗淡紅桃蕚嫰；見非是見，風搖淺碧柳絲輕；見猶離見，白雲影裏怪石露；見莫能及，流水光中古木清。莫有知時識節底麼？喝一喝。北磵和尚忌日，拈香云：監本倔強，匙挑不上。𮩸空雲蔕補虗空，陸地滔天翻白浪。暗中拈出定命竿，鶻眼鷹睛迷向當。老和尚，為誰沒齒更穿齦？從教疑殺天下人。垂寂前六日，上堂。拈拄杖卓一下，云：尋牛須見跡，諸人喫粥喫飯處、折旋俯仰處，還見跡麼？跡在牛還在，還見牛麼？直饒露逈逈地，趂亦不去，工夫純熟，皓素希奇，放行把住復由誰？嗚咿！嗚咿！擲下拄杖，云：人牛俱不見，正是月明時。小參小參結夏西天。此土多少英靈，總被二千年前一則閒公案礙塞，直是做一動子不得。眼生三角，頭峭五嶽，矢在弦上，不得不發。圓覺伽藍，入此寨，破此寨，平等性智，驢耳長，馬耳短，四稜蹋地，臭肉來蠅，又誰管你鉢盂峯雲合雲開，

Senses.Explanation: The verse says things have borne the mark of stillness since their origin. Later speakers set it against flowers, cold weather, sun, seasons, and the bustle of a retreat. Their applications ask whether stillness can be recognized within changing appearances rather than by avoiding them.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase means the patriarchs collectively: the successive figures through whom Zen records present, remember, and test the lineage. A preface describes the successive patriarchs and five houses as transmitting the same public case “like water passed from vessel to vessel,” while warning that false transmission also occurs. Juelang Daosheng offers incense for Yuantong’s founding patriarchs. Wanshan Shanshuang says every household’s window has the patriarchs, and Dahui says that after awakening he found that the buddhas and patriarchs had not deceived people.

Senses.PreferredTarget: The cause of every suffering has craving as its root
SearchAliases: the cause of every suffering has craving as its root
Senses.Note: A scriptural line says that craving is the root of suffering. Erzhan voices it before a congregation occupied with carrying stones and soil, then asks what they still want as a support. Jiqi uses the line after a pause in a sermon and turns on the question of what one is trying to obtain. Miyin explicitly quotes the Buddha while discussing clinging to body and consciousness; Shishuang makes the same citation in a wider account of wandering through lives. The two halves of the inherited teaching connect the cause of suffering to releasing the urge to grasp, while each sermon sets a different immediate test.

Senses.Explanation: The passing-stanza of the Chan records, the last word borrowed from the final rest: all fashioned things passing — the law of birth and death; birth and death done with, stillness is joy — raised at every bier and turned with circle, whisk, shout, and song. Faxi Yin lifts the incense for the titled lady: the old saying — the stanza — and birth and death set aside: what is the titled lady's stillness-enjoyment, in the end? He draws the circle and answers: one stretch of lasting light, without now or ancient; sitting free in the heaven of easy joy on the precious lotus — and the incense is burned. Mixing Jiren seats the departed layman on the whisk-tip: entered into the great bright treasury's right reception, muttering for everyone — the stanza; then the shout: struck by one shout of Zhongxing, he gallops the buddha-hall, walks into your skulls, enters the unthinkable spotless freedom-king steadiness, and sings: Bean Hill beats the tile-drum, Qi turns to Lu, three watches three points the sun overhead — the sweet is sweet, the bitter bitter. Xiaotang takes the bier-talk for the official's father: a sigh for the floating life — a tangle of affairs like hemp; even heaven's blessing a flower in the mirror — therefore it is said: the stanza. The old worthy who trusted this kicks over the sea of karma, points through the gate of the affections, knots the lotus society in the Three-Gathering hall — now he lets go and walks, nothing holding him. Qibai Defu faces the spirit of the laywoman: old Gautama said — the stanza; from the ancestors on, all bobbed head-out head-under in the birth-and-death sea, each wanting the person to cut straight through and take it on — yet you will not turn the light back, wandering birth and death. Hills and rivers, sun and stars, light and dark, form and emptiness, the four births and six kinds, sentient and insentient, what this mountain monk says and what you hear — all one conjuring. Liaozong Chaojian presses the hall three times on the closing line: do you know the news of stillness-joy? Know it — no coming, no going, no birth, no death, no right, no wrong, no this, no that, down to the four births and six kinds and all beings — nothing not stilled. Since it is so: the lady of the high house, offered for today — where has she gone? A long pause: the moon sets, the pool keeps no shadow; clouds rise, the mountain puts on its clothes.

Senses.Explanation: Dayu Shouzhi answers “what is buddha?” with “saw apart a steelyard weight.” Later masters preserve the physically resistant image while warning that turning the phrase into a ready-made idea is itself conceptual thought; the resistance does not make the weight merely unreal. Four works preserve the headword in complete local sentences rather than as an unanchored quotation. The saying turns a dense everyday object into an answer-demanding impossibility: ordinary tools cannot open what has no seam. The gloss stays at the level supported by those uses; it does not import a fixed religious resolution from outside the corpus.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ：「借路經過。」師便打。進云：「某甲通身是病，乞師一接。」師復打。自閒覺禪師語錄卷第四自閒覺禪師語錄卷第五住荊溪芙蓉寺嗣法門人住古堯乾明寺嗣法門人洪暹編拈古頌古拈古頌古舉：「世尊因自恣日，文殊三處過夏，迦葉欲白椎擯出。纔拈推，乃見百千萬億文殊，迦葉盡其神力，椎不能舉。世尊遂問迦葉：『汝擬擯那箇文殊？』迦葉無對。」拈云：「文殊三處移場過夏，固是不遵律儀；迦葉擬欲白椎擯出，不妨法令森嚴。惜乎舉而不行，累他世尊大師入泥入水。芙蓉若作迦葉，待云：『汝欲擯那箇文殊？』但擲下椎云：『罪不重科。』雖然，秪如百千萬億文殊，畢竟那箇是真底？」頌曰：「三處移場太放癡，白椎擯出令無私，當時若據今時令，百萬文殊只一椎。」舉：「趙州到臨濟，洗腳次，濟便問：『如何是祖師西來意？』州曰：『恰值山僧洗腳。』濟近前作聽勢，州曰：『會則便會，啗啄作麼？』濟便歸方丈。州曰：『三十年行腳，今日錯為人下註腳。』」拈云：「這兩箇漢大似普州人，羅漢若見，便與一坑埋卻。何故？鷸蚌相持，俱落漁人之手。」頌曰：「尖頭屋遇鬼頭風，一陣西來一陣東，開得眼來天大曉，殘花零落滿溪紅。」舉：「興化上堂云：『若是作家戰將，便請單刀直入，更莫如何若何！』有旻德長老出禮拜，起便喝，化亦喝；德又喝，化亦喝。德禮拜歸眾，化云：『適來若是別人，三十棒一棒也較不得。何故？為他旻德會一喝不作一喝用。』」拈云：「旻德按劍上來，興化亞鎗相待，然雖韜略俱全，不免如何若何。秪如興化道：『適來若是別人，三十棒一棒也較不得。為他旻德會一喝不作一喝。』又作麼生？」良久云：「鐵蛇橫古路，一馬生三寅。」頌曰：「八陣圖圓勿擬猜，衝雲攫霧應時來，功標不獨凌霄閣，別有威名壑眾才。」舉：「百丈一日問黃檗：『甚處去來？』檗云：『大雄山下採菌子來。』丈云：『還見大蟲麼？』檗便作虎聲，丈拈斧作斫勢，檗即打丈一掌，丈吟吟而笑，便歸。上堂曰：『大雄山下有一大蟲，汝等諸人也須好看，百丈老漢今日親遭一口。』」拈云：「猛虎口中奪食、飢鷹爪下分兔則且止，汝等還見百丈老漢麼？」驀拈拄杖，一時打散。頌曰：「驀然撞著南山虎，磕落雙牙和血吞，歸去不堪明示眾，雙眉愁斷雨昏昏。」舉：「百丈再參因緣，謂黃檗曰：『佛法不是小事，我當時被馬大師一喝，直得三日耳聾。』黃檗不覺吐舌。」拈云：「一盲引眾盲。」頌曰

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 錯了也。今日是冬至佳節，群陰剝盡之時，葭管灰飛，為識陽回宇宙；蓂莢榮枯，祇緣晦朔依時。乾坤變態無私，日月循環匪異。是故是，只如群陰欲去未去、一陽欲來未來，正當恁麼時，合作麼生道？庭前凍竹翻新浪，溪畔寒梅吐冷煙。」復舉：「徑山散木禪師。因巡漕雲浦蘇公問：『鴛鴦繡出從君看，不把金鍼度與人。如何是金鍼？』山曰：『我在京師走一遭，不曾遇著一人。』公擬進語，山曰：『金鍼失也。』」師云：「徑山祖翁好沒道理。蘇公問的金鍼，何得拈箇無孔鐵錘示之？雖然，別寶須是碧眼胡，不遇其人真箇苦。天劍大師遠離楚國，過訪雙林，不惜衣珍，為眾請法。苟非其人，曷能為哉？大眾！既遇其人，還識金鍼麼？」顧左右，云：「山僧不惜脣皮，為汝諸人道破。劍公是徑山祖翁第四世孫。」晚參。舉：「道吾因趙州過訪，吾著豹皮褌，把吉撩棒，在三門前等候。纔見州來，便高聲唱喏而立。州曰：『小心祇候著。』吾又唱喏一聲而去。」師云：「道吾因文攻義，趙州就窩行劫。雙林據令而行，各與烏藤三十。何故？鷸蚌相持，俱落漁人之手。」上堂。「蹋破飯床，不是尋常供養；打開布袋，祇原別示佳珍。明明聲色全彰，歷歷見聞不昧，大展光明幢，永鎮無為地，三世諸佛斫額，一切眾生倚憑。」乃豎拂子，云：「還端的麼？萬籟有心聞不得，孤巖無耳卻知音。」上堂。舉：「曹山本寂禪師，一日聞鐘聲，乃曰：『啊㖿啊㖿。』僧問：『和尚作甚麼？』山曰：『打著我心。』僧無語。徑山琇曰：『賊不打自招。』清化嶾曰：『沒量大人卻向聲色裏鼓弄人家男女。』」師云：「曹山捏鼻偷香，這僧白日著賊。徑山恁麼道也是普州人，祇有清化猶較些子。何謂？大功雖是前賢事，肝膽何妨此日傾？」晚參。舉百丈野狐因緣，師云：「不落因果，開眼也著；不昧因果，合眼也著。雖然款段無私，檢點太殺漏逗。你等還知漏逗處麼？直饒緇素分明，未出野狐圈繢。」上堂。舉：「白雲子祥禪師問僧：『不壞假名而談實相，你作麼生會？』僧指椅子曰：『這箇是椅子。』祥以手撥椅，曰：『與我將鞋袋來。』僧無對。祥曰：『這虛頭漢。』雲門偃聞曰：『須是他始得。』」師云：「蜀桐秦鏡，氣質匪常。鑒影發聲，初無二致。惜乎曲高和寡，致使風吹別調。要得條理始終，雲門未免其責。何故？不合將下里巴歌，指作陽春白雪。」臘八，上堂。僧問：「盧行者負舂，功高蓋代；丹霞老燒佛，千古流芳。未審

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 下。師拈云：「者僧到即到，只是鼻孔礙卻眼睛；九峰得即得，只有殺人刀，且無活人劍。我不似九峰，爭得到者裏？僧無語，遂喚：『上座是甚麼？』若擬議，擲下拄杖，歸方丈。」頌：遠涉誠不易，衲僧多意氣，動步即不難，腳瘦艸鞋寬。不動步，卻多般，到來豈借他人力？卻笑無端被眼瞞。慈明問楊岐：「馬祖見讓和尚便悟去，迷卻在甚麼處？」岐云：「要悟卻易，要迷卻難。」師拈云：「者箇陷人坑子，天下人不奈何，致使祖禰不了，殃及兒孫。楊岐雖善機宜，未免爛泥有刺。神鼎則不然，迷卻在甚麼處？但云：『迷即且置，把將悟的來看。』饒慈明具廣長舌，只好道一半。」頌：悟卻易，迷卻難，眨上眉毛君自看。迷悟兩途俱坐斷，月移花影上欄干。雪峰示眾云：「世界闊一尺，古鏡闊一尺；世界闊一丈，古鏡闊一丈。」玄沙指火爐云：「者箇闊多少？」峰云：「如古鏡闊。」沙云：「者箇老漢腳跟未點地在。」師拈云：「雪峰水中撈月，玄沙掉棒打月，世界古鏡火爐，都成眼中之屑。若於勝負摶量，敢保驢年未徹。畢竟如何？鷸蚌相持，俱落漁人之手。」頌：世界寬，古鏡闊，無端雪老多饒舌。石人拊掌笑咍咍，洎被將龜證作鱉。老玄沙，能勦絕，火爐句子別生涯，無限風光俱漏泄。雪峰因閩王封柑、橘各一顆，遣使送至，柬問云：「既是一般顏色，為甚麼名字不同？」峰遂依舊封回。王復馳問玄沙，沙將一張紙蓋卻。師拈云：「兩箇漢被閩王一拶，互相熱瞞，直得尾巴露出。撿點將來，總是用盡自己心，笑破他人口。」頌：柑橘一色兮誰別呼名，眾生顛倒兮逐物迷真。一般油麵兮造作由人，暗機旋合兮輥芥投針。曹溪波浪如相似，無限平人被陸沉。雪峰因閩王施銀交床，僧問：「和尚受大王如此供養，將何報答？」峰以手托地云：「少打我。」有僧舉問疏山：「雪峰少打我，意作麼生？」山云：「頭上插瓜虀，垂尾腳跟齊。」師拈云：「者一隊漢大似傍若無人，當時見雪峰恁麼時，但云：『者老漢習氣也不除。』更待疏山言了，只向道：『幸自可憐生。用頭上安頭作麼？』若更眼目定動，便掀倒禪床。且道山僧意作麼生？從前汗馬無人識，只要重論蓋代功。」頌：四稜踏地，頭角撐天。知音獨諳，玉轉珠圓。三盞酒裝公子面，一枝花扮美人妍。南院因僧問：「古殿重興時如何？」院云：「明堂瓦插簷。」僧云：「與麼則莊嚴畢備也。」院云：「斬艸蛇頭落。」師拈云：「古殿重興時，淨地上不可撒屎撒尿

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 鷸蚌相持，俱落漁人之手

Senses.Explanation: Two opponents lock together and a third party catches both. Baichi and Qianyan use the proverb to assess older contests of response and counterresponse. Zixian, Wenmu, and Yikui likewise apply it to paired contestants instead of awarding a simple victory.
